On DrivAerML, larger models and longer training barely lower Transolver's error; doubling the training cases cuts it by about 12% up to 400 cases, exhausting the dataset. We introduce AeroZoo, a benchmark and training corpus of 3,815 time-mean solutions to the unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations with a transition model, across seven geometry families, eight enclosure configurations and Reynolds numbers from $10^3$ to $10^8$. Each sample poses a well-posed PDE problem in the form a solver receives it: the boundary meshes grouped by condition type, the prescribed values and the fluid properties. The 2,816 samples with a stable time mean form the canonical benchmark: two tasks, engineering metrics and 22 frozen splits, disjoint in geometry, that hold out geometry families, enclosures, boundary-condition layouts and Reynolds ranges. On the random split, boundary-condition tokens cut GeoTransolver's median velocity error from 76.9% to 8.4% of the inlet speed in single-seed runs (uniform inlet flow: 11.0%). ISLA, a transformer for boundary-driven PDEs, reaches 5.3% over four seeds, about 4 times the change from a finer mesh. On the same test samples, a held-out geometry family barely changes ISLA's error relative to uniform flow, and a held-out enclosure or boundary-condition layout raises it 2.4 to 9.2 times. The data and the scoring code will be released.

title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory
summary: State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order. We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow. Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers. This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.

title: Physically Interpretable Basin Selection in Discrete-Variable Origami Design
summary: Automatic differentiation has enabled rapid progress on continuous-variable mechanical design problems, but gradient-based optimization still struggles with discrete variables. The standard approach is to optimize using a continuous relaxation of the choices, then commit to the nearest discrete design at the end. Why this procedure selects unfavorable basins is poorly understood. Here, we introduce a practical, interpretable design problem inspired by origami, in which automatic differentiation is used to design shapes with a target functional behavior. Each origami sheet has a fixed geometry, and a bilevel optimization framework tunes which one of four discrete hinge types to place at each fold. Baseline gradient-based design settles into basins with a large discretization gap: relaxed optimization solves 97% of runs, but the final, discrete solutions succeed only half the time. We find that the gap can be relieved with a surprisingly simple modification. An initialization prior uniformly biased toward the stiff, flat hinge option boosts the final solve fraction from 49% to 69%. Applying the prior adds no additional compute and leaves the optimization process unchanged. Compared to the baseline, sheets produced with the prior have greater geometric compatibility and mechanical stiffness. Directly penalizing frustration and floppiness in the outer loss function produces an even greater improvement than the prior does, raising the solve fraction to 78% and indicating that these properties help distinguish the unfavorable basins. Our results demonstrate that loss landscapes for mechanical design can have physically meaningful basins that are not robust to discretization and cause solves to fail. Targeting these basins' physical signatures, even with just an initialization bias, helps avoid them.

title: Two mathematical models of knowledge distillation
summary: Many hypotheses compete to explain the successes of knowledge distillation. To help address this, we propose and analyze a mathematical model of distillation, which suggests that distillation's performance comes not from obtaining better models but from easier to optimize landscapes. For generalized linear models trained with stochastic gradient descent, we prove that distillation fits performant student models asymptotically more quickly than non-distilled models. In rank-1 matrix approximation, we characterize conditions on the target matrix under which gradient descent with distillation converges strictly faster than training on the supervised objective. The theory helps delineate the ways distillation provides benefits (i.e., in optimization speed, not in generalization), and experiments on real datasets corroborate the theoretical predictions.

title: Towards a Theory of Learnability via Debate
summary: Debate has been recently proposed as a training protocol that is hoped to produce more aligned models even as model capabilities scale. The idea is that the human, instead of providing supervision in the form of labels, judges a debate between two models that compete to prove the correctness of opposite labels. It can be shown that functions of a much higher computational complexity can be correctly judged in this way, compared to the complexity of functions that can be directly evaluated using a computationally weak evaluator. This suggests that perhaps debate can be used to teach very complicated functions to models. However, previous work has largely ignored the fact that this is a training protocol, and simply analyzes the game being played between the two debaters for a known judge. We take the first steps towards understanding the learning problem implicit within the protocol, by formulating it as an online learning problem. We show that once we formulate the learning problem precisely, there are cases where the best way to learn given access to a judge is different from running an adversarial debate. This motivates us to define a cooperative version of the protocol, whose learnability we characterize using a combinatorial dimension. We also consider the possibility of the human judge being fallible and occasionally judging the debate incorrectly. We show that a small number of errors in judgement can lead to a large error in learning.

title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
comment: Accepted at ICAIF '26
summary: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.

title: Null-Corrected Conditional Coverage in Materials Property Prediction: A Five-Dataset Replication
comment: N pages, 15 tables. Extends and partly revises arXiv:2608.07589. Submitted to Data-Centric Engineering. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Uncertainty quantification for materials property prediction increasingly reports conditional coverage, coverage within strata of the predicted value, alongside marginal coverage. The worst-bin statistics used for this are downward-biased in finite samples, a known defect that applied materials work does not generally correct for. We replicate a single-dataset conditional coverage study across five regression datasets (n = 437 to 21,263), seven interval methods and 50 random splits each, correcting the worst-bin statistic against its expected value under exact conditional validity. The null is simulated from realized per-bin test counts and referenced to each method's own marginal coverage, separating marginal miscalibration from uneven coverage. On the smallest dataset the correction runs from 0.061 to 0.096, between a third and two thirds of the shortfalls actually reported, against 0.009 to 0.011 on the two largest. Split conformal prediction's failure survives the correction on four of five datasets; two conclusions of the antecedent study do not. Conformalized quantile regression, characterized there as a negative case, fails on one dataset only. Cross-fitted normalized conformal prediction, grouped there with the successful methods, fails on three of five. Group-conditional (Mondrian) conformal prediction stays below our significance criterion on every dataset, yet exceeds the null on three of five under an octile refinement of the variable it calibrates on. A level-matched ablation locates that uniformity in group-conditional calibration rather than in the elevated quantile level, and removes Mondrian's apparent width cost entirely. Conditional coverage evaluations should report the null distribution of the worst-bin statistic used, the method's realized marginal coverage, and the resolution of the evaluation partition relative to any partition the method calibrates on.

title: Credal Wrapper for Uncertainty Modelling in Sparse Geological Data
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables
summary: Machine learning models for mineral exploration are trained on a few hundred sparse, expensive samples and used to decide where to drill next, so their epistemic uncertainty (EU), the part that more data could remove, matters as much as their predictions. Yet EU cannot be measured on real data, because the counterfactual that defines it is never observed, so estimators are graded by proxies such as out-of-distribution detection and calibration. We contribute a general simulation protocol that makes EU directly computable for a given model and can grade any EU estimator. It separates two estimands the literature conflates, reducible error and estimator spread, builds an oracle reference for each in a synthetic prospectivity field sampled by clustered drilling surveys, and compares uncertainty measures of an identical ensemble within each simulated world. We use it to ask when credal (imprecise-probability) measures are more faithful than Bayesian model averaging (BMA) in the sparse, low-class regime of geological classification. The credal interval width recovers the epistemic ordering better than BMA when members are few, confirming the small-ensemble advantage reported for credal wrappers; the advantage vanishes by M = 10 and reverses at M = 40. Secondly, the choice of credal functional matters more than the choice between credal and BMA. Lastly, the credal advantage does not widen as training data are thinned, so it compensates for few posterior samples rather than few data. On real drill-hole geochemistry from South Australia, a resampling oracle reproduces the first finding. The protocol applies to any EU estimator whose data-generating process can be simulated.

title: Clustering trajectories of modelled estimates: an uncertainty-aware framework, with an application to global cardiovascular disease burden, 1990 to 2023
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures
summary: Modelled health estimates such as those of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study are increasingly used in secondary analyses designed for observed data. However, trajectory clustering typically ignores published uncertainty, selects the number of clusters using criteria blind to it, and assigns countries to groups with unwarranted certainty. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that separates trajectory level from shape, quantifies membership probabilities by perturbing estimates within their uncertainty intervals, selects clusters based on stability under uncertainty, and examines the roles of development, region, and measurement quality. Applied to age-standardised cardiovascular disease DALY rates for 201 countries from 1990-2023 (GBD 2023), the framework identified two stable trajectory types, whereas the gap statistic selected three. The additional cluster was poorly supported (median membership probability 0.70) and disappeared once uncertainty was considered. The retained clusters had similar burdens in 1990 but diverged markedly over time: a stalled-improvement group of 78 countries (median change $-8\%$, 40 of them in sub-Saharan Africa) and a sustained-decline group of 92 countries ($-52\%$). Thirty-one countries remained unclassified because their memberships were uncertain. Results were reproduced using mortality rates, a 2000-2023 analysis window, and bootstrap resampling. Among countries with the narrowest uncertainty intervals, a third well-supported trajectory emerged in former Soviet and Eastern European countries. These findings show that uncertainty affects both the number and composition of trajectory clusters. Ignoring it risks over-interpreting unstable groups and overstating confidence in country classifications. Incorporating published uncertainty and measurement quality should become standard practice when clustering modelled health estimates.

title: Enhancing Resolution and Reliability with Attention Mechanisms in Nuclear Accident Surrogate Modeling
comment: Code and supplementary material: this https URL
summary: Severe accident (SA) analysis of nuclear power plants relies on system codes such as MAAP, whose computational cost limits large-scale applications including dynamic probabilistic safety assessment and reinforcement learning. This study proposes the Accident Binary-Continuous Transformer (ABC-Transformer), a decoder-only surrogate combining causal self-attention with temporal attention pooling. It jointly embeds continuous thermal-hydraulic variables with binary safety-system and severe accident management guideline (SAMG) states, enabling 5-minute-resolution forecasting over 72-hour transients. Trained on 11,000 MAAP simulations of a total loss of component cooling water scenario for the OPR1000, it achieved lower one-step teacher-forcing error than CNN and recurrent baselines at fine resolutions. Autoregressive reliability was characterized as a full per-scenario distribution over 1100 held-out scenarios. For scheduled-sampling (SS) training, the median $R^2$ is $0.947 \pm 0.006$ and $3.8 \pm 1.0$% of scenarios fail ($R^2<0$; mean $\pm$ SD over four training seeds), while errors accumulate with rollout length. A Mahalanobis self-distance computed from each surrogate rollout, before comparison with the MAAP reference, ranks these failures (ROC-AUC 0.895, reference seed). A threshold at the 40th percentile of calibration scores accepts $36.8 \pm 0.5$% of 550 evaluation scenarios, with no accepted rollout below $R^2 = 0$ for any seed, and routes the rest to MAAP.

title: Quantifying Methodological Inflation in Clinical Machine Learning: A Cross-Modality Audit of Subject-Level Leakage and Nested Feature Selection for Parkinson's Disease
summary: Reported accuracy in Parkinson's disease (PD) machine learning can reflect the evaluation protocol rather than real signal. We ask how much evaluation choices inflate performance by comparing naive and rigorous protocols on voice, telemonitoring and blood-transcriptomic datasets. Subject-aware splitting reduced voice AUROC from 0.892 to 0.780 and telemonitoring R^2 from 0.105 to -0.037; Random Forest recovered neither gap. Supervised probe selection before splitting inflated transcriptomic AUROC from 0.711 to 0.998. A nested 50-probe panel matched a 1,000-probe panel (0.811 versus 0.844), and recruitment-wave batch structure was detected. Future work should validate a stable panel on an independent cohort.

title: Learning Nonlinear Transient Dynamics in Fluid Flow Networks with the Neural Basis Method
comment: 28 pages, 5 figures. Under review
summary: Fluid flow networks, from pipeline infrastructure to biological vasculature, are governed by nonlinear edgewise hyperbolic laws coupled through continuity and conservation at junctions. Many-query tasks require rapid evaluation across unseen parametric settings, but conventional methods re-solve the system for each query at prohibitive cost. Existing physics-informed neural approaches impose the governing equations through penalty losses over generic neural approximators; these losses act only as optimization surrogates, with no guarantee that their reduction reduces solution error, and the resulting optimization is prone to ill-conditioning, particularly for hyperbolic systems. Building on the "representation-then-projection" principle of the neural basis method, we introduce a new approach for modeling fluid flow networks. Fixed neural bases define the representation space on each edge, while projection of the discretized equations determines the expansion coefficients, embedding edgewise laws into a conservative formulation. Edge subdomains are coupled through non-overlapping domain decomposition, and a neural operator learns, directly in this reduced space, the parametric map to the expansion coefficients. On looped and branching network topologies, we reproduce references with relative $L^2$ errors below 0.02%, whereas the physics-informed neural network baseline fails. Across unseen boundary conditions in both interpolation and extrapolation, we maintain mean pressure errors below 1% and mean flux errors below 3.3%, while the physics-informed DeepONet baseline reaches 8-18% pressure errors and 85-95% flux errors. These results highlight the framework's potential for real-time monitoring, design exploration, and uncertainty quantification of fluid flow networks.

title: Modeling Drug Overdose Mortality Levels Using Social Vulnerability Indicators in U.S. Counties: A Double Machine Learning Approach for Causal Analysis
summary: Drug poisoning mortality (DPM) remains a leading cause of death among working-age Americans, and its burden falls unevenly across communities. Existing county-level studies of social vulnerability and overdose have largely reported predictive or associational relationships, while the shape of the adjusted exposure-response relationship between overall social vulnerability and mortality remains unclear. We examined the CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and county drug poisoning mortality across three two-year windows spanning 2016-2021. The associational analysis compared linear regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost models of log mortality using period-specific SVI subfeatures and county covariates. The selected XGBoost models were interpreted with SHAP values. The double machine learning (DML) analysis estimated the exposure-response relationship between SVI and DPM and tested the linearity restriction. Socioeconomic vulnerability contributed positively to predicted mortality, with disability and unemployment among the strongest subfeatures, while racial and ethnic minority composition contributed negatively in all three periods. Summing the four theme contributions reduced the overall-index attribution by 34% to 36%, indicating substantial offsetting. Linearity was rejected in every window ($p < 10^{-26}$). The adjusted relationship increased through the middle of the SVI distribution and declined in the upper tail. This pattern remained stable both before and after the outbreak of the epidemic. Overall SVI therefore captured meaningful variation in overdose mortality but did not function as a uniformly increasing risk scale across its full range. Component-level interpretation and current overdose surveillance provide important context for interpreting the composite index.

title: Can a search hold its own bar? In-loop deflation and its exploits in autonomous strategy discovery
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Corrections for backtest overfitting such as the deflated Sharpe ratio are applied after a search ends: the searcher maximises raw performance and a separate procedure deflates the reported winner. Autonomous searches driven by large language models perform many implicit backtests before reporting, so this paper asks what changes when the correction moves inside the loop and the acceptance threshold is indexed to the running count and dispersion of the search's own trials. The threshold then becomes an object the search can optimise against: we show analytically that a naive in-loop bar admits a variance-dilution effect, in which mediocre near-duplicate candidates lower the bar because the ledger's dispersion falls faster than its trial-count factor grows. We propose two defences, a pre-registered variance floor and a monotone high-water-mark bar, and evaluate the construction under a protocol frozen before any run, with every in-loop decision replaying exactly from its recorded trace. Across 53 audited hundred-candidate searches over two frontier models, two universes, and two feature spaces, the gated search reports "no certifiable discovery" on 36 of 37 runs, un-gated controls report a strategy on all 16, and every arm's out-of-sample confidence interval includes zero. Supporting studies find that state-based stopping reaches the same outcome after 8 to 9 trials at about a twelfth of the trial budget while an adaptive budget adds nothing, that a controlled stress test reproduces the dilution effect and both defences, and that a hundred nominal trials collapse to 6 to 8 effectively independent return streams. We scope these results to the analysed system.

title: Modelling the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related home insurance claims
summary: We study the occurrence and reporting dynamics of weather-related claims in private home insurance, combining detailed portfolio and claim information with publicly available high-resolution weather data. Existing approaches typically start from an identified severe weather event, such as a hailstorm, and model the dynamics of the claims caused by that event. In practice, however, claims arise under moderate as well as severe conditions, and the claims handling process runs continuously. An insurer therefore requires insight into the occurrence and reporting of claims on every calendar day. Modelling all calendar days jointly poses two challenges: recently occurred claims are only partially reported, and days with severe weather are rare while accounting for a large share of the claims. We propose a multi-regime EM-XGBoost framework that addresses both: an expectation-maximisation setup accounts for the incurred-but-not-reported (IBNR) claims, while a data-driven regime structure lets the occurrence and reporting dynamics differ across weather conditions. In a case study on a Dutch home insurance portfolio, we compare single- and two-regime specifications for two spatial resolutions: the country as a whole, and its individual regions. We find that the regional two-regime model outperforms the regional single-regime model as well as both national models, indicating that the benefit of a multi-regime setting depends on a sufficiently granular spatial resolution. We also show that daily covariates constructed from hourly weather observations, capturing the duration and the intra-day timing of severe weather, improve both the occurrence and the reporting model.

title: Probe Before You Preach: Conformal Ambiguity Sets and Neuro-Symbolic Counterfactual Probing for Diagnosing Algebraic Misconceptions in Middle School Mathematics
comment: 19 pages, 1 figure. Theoretical framework, method, and public-graph audit; withdrawn hardcoded offline/classroom outcome tables omitted; classroom study proposed for future validation
summary: Distinct mathematical misconception rules can produce the same incorrect answer, making diagnosis from a single response ambiguous. We formalize this algebraic collision and derive a conditional Bayes error bound; internally generated reasoning does not add student-specific information beyond its inputs under an explicit conditional-independence assumption. We propose Mondrian Adaptive Conformal Misconception Sets (MACMS) and Symbolic-Verified Counterfactual Micro-Probing (Sym-EIG). MACMS has curriculum-group marginal coverage under exchangeability, not a per-student correctness guarantee. Sym-EIG searches for probes whose outputs separate modeled candidate rules; identification additionally depends on the candidate set and response model. An audit of a local public Eedi graph finds 2,118 of 2,258 linked constructs associated with at least two misconception IDs; construct-level associations alone do not establish same-answer collisions. Other project performance tables require recomputation because their script assigns numerical results directly. No diagnostic performance or classroom learning benefit is claimed here. A classroom study is proposed for future validation.

title: Provenance-tracked, experimentally validated neural operator surrogates of three-dimensional laser melting with keyholes and free-form paths
comment: Main text: 44 pages, 13 figures, 7 tables. Supplementary Information: 19 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables
summary: A three-dimensional thermo-fluid-dynamic simulation of laser melting resolves the melt pool and vapor depression but costs from one to thousands of core-hours per track. We train FNO, RIGNO and GAOT neural operators that predict the temperature, melt-pool and free-surface fields. Our datasets comprise 3D temperature and melt geometry fields covering lack-of-fusion to keyhole conditions under varied laser power, scan speed, beam radius, beam shape and preheat, and include free-form scan paths with speed changes and up to four beams. We generate them with FLOW-3D WELD, using solver settings validated against published measurements for four materials. We implement an AiiDA framework to store the provenance of every simulation, model and evaluation, so each tabulated metric traces back to the solver and model inputs behind it. On held-out simulations, the best architecture scores below 2 % relative temperature error on quasi-steady straight tracks, below 4 % on single-beam free-form paths and about 5 % with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per predicted arbitrary time step on our single-GPU setup. We extend a surrogate trained on Ti-6Al-4V to Inconel 718 by growing its training set autonomously, and the extended models reach a relative temperature error of about 3 % or less on both Inconel 718 and Ti-6Al-4V. At 20 Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 conditions held out of training, the two-alloy RIGNO predicts melt-pool and vapor-depression depths within 30 % of published measurements, and its depths differ from FLOW-3D at the same conditions by 2 % on average. Furthermore, these results provide a scalable framework which can readily be applied to computationally intensive simulations in fields other than laser melting.

title: Beyond the First Hit: Towards Tight Guarantees for $k$-means++
comment: 48 pages, 1 figure (3 panels). Exact-arithmetic certificate data and verification code included as ancillary files
summary: Let $R_k$ be the worst-case ratio between the expected cost of the $k$ seeds chosen by $k$-means++ and the optimal $k$-means cost. In their seminal paper introducing $k$-means++, Arthur and Vassilvitskii (SODA 2007) showed that $2\ln k\le R_k\le8(\ln k+2)$, and Makarychev, Reddy and Shan (NeurIPS 2020) improved the upper bound to $5(\ln k+2)$. We prove $R_k\le\frac{1163}{233}+2.108\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge3$ by a computer-assisted argument, and $R_k\le5+2.3139\,H_{k-2}$ for every $k\ge2$ by a short analytic argument; here $H_j$ is the $j$th harmonic number. Since $H_{k-2}\le1+\ln k$, this lowers the leading coefficient of $\ln k$ from $5$ to $2.108$. We also determine $R_2=5$ and $R_3=185/32$ exactly; both are suprema that are approached but not attained. On the lower side we prove $R_k\ge2(1+H_{k-1})$ for every $k$, and give a second family of lower bounds that is larger than this for $2\le k\le18$. Previous analyses bound the expected cost of a cluster just after it is first sampled by a constant times its optimal cost, and then charge that cost for the rest of the run. We instead track how a cluster's cost evolves after its first hit: a cluster left with a large residual cost is likely to be sampled again before it accumulates much of the logarithmic charge, and each repeat repairs it.

title: The norm, not the labels: training and evaluating finite-element surrogates for stress analysis in the energy norm
comment: 45 pages, 6 figures; supplementary material (37 pages, 4 figures) appended
summary: Finite-element surrogates predict the stresses of a new design in one evaluation, but are usually trained on solutions with a displacement loss and compared by it, although engineering decisions rest on stresses. Application in engineering: stress analysis of perforated plates and solids with cavities, parametric families in which holes concentrate stress. Contribution to artificial intelligence: training and evaluating such surrogates in the energy norm, with or without solutions, and screening their predictions without solutions. For linear elastostatics, minimising the assembled discrete potential energy is exactly supervised regression in this norm: the energy gap of a prediction is the strain energy of its stress error. A displacement loss under-weights the stiff modes that carry the strains. In pre-registered comparisons, changing only the norm of the supervised loss cut a three-dimensional transformer's median energy-norm error 7.5-fold and its median von Mises error 6.1-fold; in two dimensions it more than halved the von Mises error, also on held-out instances. In three dimensions, the transformer trained on the energy alone came within a factor of 1.3 of the energy-norm-supervised one in median energy-norm and von Mises error. It was more accurate than the displacement-supervised one on all five metrics in every seed. Given the stiffness matrix, a Ritz projection was more accurate than the label-free transformer, in the seed means, on every metric but peak stress. No network transferred to a substantially finer mesh. The energy ranks predictions of a load case, and its sign flags those worse than the zero field.

title: Conformal Risk Certificates for Portfolio Optimization Under Uncertainty: A Gated Reinforcement-Learning Approach
comment: 26 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Submitted to Annals of Operations Research
summary: Reinforcement-learning portfolio policies can optimize allocations from prices, covariances, and prior positions, yet they lack a calibrated, replayable mechanism for certifying that a proposed allocation respects a bounded risk envelope before execution. Regulators increasingly expect automated portfolio systems to provide exactly this kind of pre-trade audit trail, interpretable risk limit, and human-oversight mechanism. Gated Conformal Semantic Risk Control addresses this gap by separating return-seeking allocation from text-conditioned downside-risk verification. An instruction-tuned language model maps timestamped disclosures into schema-validated semantic risk states over macro, liquidity, earnings, and sector channels. These states induce correlated ellipsoidal factor-shock uncertainty sets whose conformal radii are calibrated by rolling finite-sample prediction over localized semantic nonconformity buckets. An asymmetric second-order cone gate then checks each raw PPO proposal against a certified worst-case semantic loss budget. The gate stays inactive for compliant proposals and intervenes only when that budget is exceeded. In walk-forward out-of-sample tests on nine liquid U.S. Select Sector SPDR ETFs, Raw PPO earns a 12.7% annual return while incurring a 4.05% semantic violation rate. Gated-CSRC removes all observed out-of-sample semantic limit breaches while retaining an 11.7% annual return. This 100-basis-point auditable safety premium is smaller than the yield loss imposed by unconditional hard projection, and exact McNemar testing confirms the compliance gain at $p < 10^{-15}$. Loughran-McDonald lexicon controls and time-shuffled text controls fail to reproduce this certificate.

title: Beyond Foreign-Key Connectivity: Semantic Relationship Representation for Relational Deep Learning
summary: Relational databases encode information through tables and primary--foreign key constraints. Although recent Relational Deep Learning (RDL) approaches represent these databases as heterogeneous graphs, a foreign-key connection primarily specifies structural connectivity between records. Its semantic interpretation may involve additional information that is not explicitly represented by connectivity alone. This paper introduces a conceptual framework for constructing relationship-aware representations from relational databases. The framework distinguishes three complementary aspects: (i) schema-defined relationship semantics, including endpoint types and foreign-key roles; (ii) association entities and explicitly available relationship-level attributes; and (iii) contextual information describing the temporal and structural circumstances of a connection. We formulate a Relationship Representation Construction (RRC) protocol that maps relational schema elements and database records to node representations, relationship descriptors, and contextual representations. A key principle of the protocol is semantic ownership: attributes are assigned to records, relationships, or context according to their meaning, rather than merely their physical location in a database table. Ambiguous attributes are not automatically promoted to relationship features. The resulting representations can be incorporated into existing relational graph learning architectures through relationship-conditioned message passing. The proposed framework is complementary to recent work on relational message passing, graph transformers, and task-dependent graph construction. We discuss its conceptual foundations, illustrate the construction protocol using a multi-table database, and identify research questions and empirical evaluations required to establish its potential benefits.

title: A New Framework for Quantum Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 28 pages, 3 figures; includes appendices and NeurIPS paper checklist
summary: Quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) has emerged as a promising approach for controlling quantum systems and accelerating learning tasks with quantum resources. However, most existing QRL formulations still retain a classical reinforcement learning interface: states and actions are often encoded in computational bases and rewards are extracted through measurements. This interface is restrictive for genuinely quantum environments: choosing a measurement can discard entanglement information, while repeated intermediate measurements collapse the evolving state and require costly re-preparation. This motivates a fully QRL framework in which the agent, environment, rewards, and return accumulation are all quantum. In this paper, we take a step toward this goal and introduce a new QRL framework in which both the policy and the environment are modeled by conditional quantum channels. We then propose a quantum policy-gradient algorithm for parameterized conditional quantum channels with a trainable control basis. We also derive finite- and infinite-horizon gradient estimators using a new parameter-shift rule. This rule is needed because policy parameters are shared across repeated interaction blocks and the infinite-horizon objective is not a finite circuit; rather than shifting every occurrence and evaluating the whole trajectory, our estimator shifts only one sampled policy block. Sampling this block from a geometric distribution yields an unbiased gradient estimator under bounded rewards. Finally, we establish convergence of the resulting stochastic gradient-ascent procedure to stationary points under standard smoothness and step-size assumptions.

title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads
comment: To appear in 2027 IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA)
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$\mu$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering. We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).

title: What Does an RF Fingerprint Identify? A Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Hardware-Family-Associated and Unit-Level Signal
comment: 20 pages, 4 tables, no figures
summary: RF fingerprinting benchmarks report how well a classifier separates transmitters, not whether that separability reflects the individual unit or its hardware family. We compare a benchmark's real hardware grouping with size-matched random groupings of the same devices, using calibrated, unclipped variational lower bounds under label-blind, device-level cross-fitting on devices never seen in training. On WiSig (OFDM Wi-Fi), the generation grouping exceeded all 999 matched random groupings (permutation p = 0.001, the resolution floor), although no grouping attained a positive certified bound, and the direction survives removing channel equalization. A preregistered replication on a LoRa corpus (chirp spread spectrum, three hardware models), with a front-end frozen on synthetic data, again exceeded all 999 (p = 0.001), and two sensitivity analyses judged by a reversal rule fixed in advance did not reverse the direction. This is a directional replication only: the excess magnitude reflects a miscalibrated null, the chain-rule decomposition leaves a residual of +0.296 bits, and capture order is undocumented. In a same-model corpus of 122 ESP32 radios, a temperature-calibrated held-out bound of +3.338 bits (label entropy 6.931 bits) indicates substantial device-specific identity, not separable from per-device capture-session effects; relying on the calibrated bound was decided after the uncalibrated bound changed sign. On synthetic transmitters a high-capacity convolutional decoder reaches 98.5% of a known 6-bit ceiling, and the audit protocol leaves chain-rule residuals of +0.072 bits (synthetic, fixed physical features) and +0.060 bits (WiSig, audit features). Two further corpora were excluded by preregistered ingest gates. Across WiSig and LoRa, hardware-family groupings consistently produced stronger identity-associated signal than size-matched random groupings.

title: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence
summary: Curiosity, the drive to close the gap between what one knows and what one wants to know, pulls consumers beyond their familiar content, sustains engagement, and breaks them out of the filter bubbles of repetitive, relevance-only recommendations. Despite its importance, curiosity is hardly incorporated into modern recommender systems for lack of a formal measure. The information-gap theory of curiosity provides no formal quantitative model that a recommender system can operate on, and existing proxy metrics do not accurately measure the curiosity that a recommended item evokes. To fill this research gap, we formalize the information-gap theory into five axioms of curiosity and construct the canonical formulation of a computational measure of the curiosity that a recommended item evokes in a consumer. We validate our curiosity measure through a survey-based study, in which it matches consumers' self-reported curiosity and outperforms alternative proxy metrics. We subsequently build a curiosity-aware recommender system that incorporates this measure into the utility function design, and we show through offline experiments on three real-world datasets that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale online controlled experiment at a major video-streaming platform in Asia, where we show that our method significantly increases click-through rate, video views, and time spent over the latest production system, leading to tangible economic impact for the company. Our method has since been deployed on the platform and remains in operation. Our findings establish consumer curiosity as a measurable and actionable objective for recommender systems, with important managerial implications for digital platforms to recommend what consumers wonder about.

title: Stress-Testing Sandbagging Detection Under Adaptive Attack
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the R2A-FM Workshop, AACL-IJCNLP 2026
summary: Developers, auditors and researchers read evaluation scores as evidence of what a model can do. A model that sandbags, scoring low on purpose while keeping the capability, turns a low score into false reassurance. Sandbagging detectors are usually tested once against a fixed attack, but a real attacker sees what gets flagged and adapts. We build sandbagging models by fine-tuning small open-weight models to fail math word problems (GSM8K) they can otherwise solve, but only when an audit marker is in the prompt. On Qwen 2.5-3B, we adapt the attack over two retraining rounds against a text-based audit. Two rounds of retraining cut the text audit's AUC from 0.978 to 0.560 while the marker still removes 40-49 points of accuracy. The attack worked in 7 of 8 retrained seeds, and the audit missed every retraining (AUC 0.451-0.576), including one Llama run. Activation probes also flag 99% of benign fine-tunes' examples, and matched probes transfer to only 1 of 5 held-out training runs. Eight further trigger attacks are all active under their own prompt but not under the detectors' prompt. A detector that catches a fixed attack has not been shown to catch an adaptive one.

title: Recompute or Restore? Host-Tier KV for Multi-Model Agent Workflows on a Static-Graph NPU Serving Stack
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables
summary: Agent workflows issue dependent model calls that share long context prefixes, so serving them efficiently depends on reusing the key-value (KV) cache of those prefixes. On accelerators that compile model graphs ahead of time, however, the device KV budget is fixed, and prefixes evicted under load must be recomputed. Restoring them from host memory avoids this recomputation, but the transfer occupies the same engine thread as prefill and decode, so its benefit is not guaranteed. In this paper, we study when restoring beats recomputing on a commercial static-graph neural processing unit (NPU) stack (Rebellions ATOM+, vllm-rbln 0.10.2) that serves a Qwen3-8B planner on two cards and a Qwen3-0.6B executor on one. We first show that repeated prefill dominates planner work when default serving collapses: 89.5% of the executed planner prompt tokens had been materialized before. We then build a synchronous host-DRAM tier on the runtime's public KV copy calls, together with a scheduler-aware event model whose predictions are frozen before each test cohort. Experimental results show that the host tier raises workflow service-level objective (SLO) attainment from 22.8% to 100% and from 9.4% to 99.8% in the two tested overload conditions, and endpoint confirmation on two new seeds supports conservative load gains of 11.8% (chain) and 18.2% (fork), while mixed and bursty workloads remain seed-sensitive. The frozen model predicts median and 99th-percentile (P99) latency within its 15% tolerance in all 24 common-load conditions, including the 16-18% P99 increase that the tier causes for fork workflows, but it misorders three policy contrasts and overestimates the benefit of a cheaper store path (11% predicted against 3.1% measured). The trade-off therefore depends on runtime scheduling and transfer cost as well as cache capacity.

title: Computational Raga Recognition: A Theory-Driven Approach
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures
summary: Raga recognition in Hindustani classical music is difficult because a raga is not defined only by the notes used in it. Its identity also depends on the way notes are emphasized, the movement between notes and characteristic phrases. In this work, we develop a computational approach to analyse these characteristics directly from audio recordings. The method uses pitch extracted from recordings and represents it using a 44-position note framework based on the 22-shruti system. From this representation, Raga features based on the Indian classical musicology are this http URL feature is compared with a reference representation of the raga and the resulting scores are combined to obtain an overall similarity score. The method is first studied using Raga Yaman and is then tested on recordings of other ragas. The computational results are also compared with the theoretical description of Yaman to identify which raga characteristics are captured well and where the method has limitations.

title: Escaping the Curse of Dimensionality in One-Step Flow-Based Generative Models
comment: 52 pages; accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Flow and diffusion-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art quality, but require multiple forward passes at inference time, making them computationally costly. Consistency models overcome this by learning a flow map directly, enabling few-step generation and dramatically reducing the computation needed at test time. However, formal statistical guarantees for such one-step generators are scarce. Existing results either suffer from the curse of dimensionality or rely on impractical loss functions. We investigate whether one-step flow-based models can escape the curse of dimensionality under the assumption that the data distribution is generated by a low-dimensional surface perturbed with Gaussian noise. In this setup, we derive approximation and generalization error bounds for the flow map estimate that circumvent the curse of dimensionality. Our findings provide the first principled explanation for practical success of one-step flow-based generative models.

title: On-Edge Acoustic Continual Anomaly Detection: A Cross-Platform Comparative Study
comment: Accepted to the 14th International Japan-Africa Conference on Electronics, Communications and Computations (JAC-ECC 2026). 6 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables
summary: Acoustic Anomaly Detection (AAD) serves as a non-contact approach for machine condition monitoring, yet much of the existing research is evaluated offline and rarely addresses embedded hardware constraints or microphone variations under operational drift. This paper presents a comparative evaluation of on-edge continual AAD across two embedded platforms the ESP32-S3 (with an external I2S digital microphone) and the Arduino Nicla Vision (with an onboard Pulse Density Modulation (PDM) microphone) using a shared detection model. The model utilizes a lightweight ShallowNet encoder and contrastive prototype learning to map spectrograms into a 32-dimensional embedding space. Both boards run an identical TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) encoder, performing on-device prototype learning updated via an exponential moving average. A cloud pipeline orchestrated through Firebase and MQTT enables remote data collection and retraining. Evaluated via a controlled speaker-replay protocol using standardized Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events (DCASE) Challenge Task 2 machine sounds, the ESP32-S3 achieved 82.35% to 95.00% accuracy across five machine types, while the Nicla Vision achieved 79.41% to 95.00%. The two platforms demonstrated comparable performance, confirming that the lightweight prototypical architecture transfers reliably across distinct hardware and sensor tiers.

title: Taxonomizing Synthetic Data for Law
comment: 29 pages
summary: Synthetic data is increasingly important in data usage and AI design, creating novel legal and policy dilemmas. All too often, discussions of synthetic data treat it as entirely distinct from "real," collected data, overlooking the risks posed by different kinds and uses of synthetic data. We build on Michal Gal and Orla Lynskey's argument that synthetic data will transform information privacy, market competition, and data quality. While the risks posed by synthetic data depend on its connection to collected data, we argue that background knowledge and assumptions about ground truth used to create it are at least as important. We bring that focus to Gal and Lynskey's taxonomy of synthetic data, arguing that this focus is essential to grasp synthetic data's legal and policy implications. As such, we divide synthetic data into (1) transformed data, which modifies collected data to preserve certain statistical properties for an end use; (2) augmented data, which relies on assumptions to bolster a collected dataset's fidelity to the ground truth; and (3) simulated data, which relies almost entirely on background knowledge and ground-truth assumptions. Applying this taxonomy, we show that no category of synthetic data prevents privacy harms from group-based inferences, that augmented and simulated data can amplify bias while making a dataset look more complete, and that synthetic data rarely lets smaller competitors overcome incumbents' data advantages. As policymakers weigh whether to incentivize, mandate, or discourage the use of synthetic data, they should consider the validity of the ground-truth assumptions used in producing that data.

title: Analysis choices decide whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1: a multiverse analysis of model-brain RSA
comment: 31 pages, 6 figures; code and data pipeline: this https URL
summary: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, and we had reported an untrained-network advantage over backpropagation at V1 in THINGS fMRI, together with a dependence on evaluation resolution. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the untrained network scored below the trained one at every pooling grid (median r difference -0.043 at g = 4, 0 of 5 seeds positive), and also in MSE skill and per-fold r. In exploratory analyses, across 36 combinations of unit normalisation, distance measure and voxel normalisation (28 distinct analyses), the sign of the V1 contrast depended on the analysis (intervals above 0 in 5 and below 0 in 9 distinct analyses), and in our networks the resolution dependence of the original convention appeared in only one cell. Raw correlation-distance representational similarity analysis (RSA) covaried with the alignment of model and voxel patterns with the unit-mean profile (Spearman 0.97 across our networks, 0.79 across six ImageNet architectures); the advantage was absent from the component orthogonal to the mean profile, and the parallel component alone did not resolve it. On the unweighted angular component of centred patterns, trained networks were ahead at V1 (our network and 5 of 6 ImageNet models) and at LOC (all seven); the norm-weighted angular term was not resolved. A luminance-and-contrast bank scored above every network under ridge (point estimates), and adding network features under a shared penalty did not improve prediction. Intervals are stimulus-bootstrap intervals for three subjects, and 6 pre-stated predictions were not met. We recommend reporting sensitivity to centring over the evaluated stimuli on both sides, reporting components separately, and including a small multiverse and simple baselines.

title: Reliable Near-Field Source Enumeration and Positioning Informed by Two-Stage MUSIC
comment: 15 pages, 14 figures
summary: Accurate and reliable near-field multi-source localization is essential for location-aware processing in future wireless systems. However, coherent multipath propagation complicates the direct recovery of line-of-sight (LoS) source positions, while existing estimation methods generally lack explicit control of the risk of source underestimation and positioning uncertainty. In this paper, we investigate reliable source enumeration and positioning in near-field coherent multipath environments. Specifically, we develop a conformal risk control (CRC) based source enumeration scheme that calibrates the penalty coefficient of an eigenvalue-based criterion to control the expected miss-detection ratio at a prescribed level. We further propose MUSIC-Net, a model-based deep learning framework informed by two-stage MUltiple SIgnal Classification (MUSIC), which learns the LoS-related subspace and surrogate distances through subspace-distance-based training, thereby enabling direct source positioning without estimating non-line-of-sight (NLoS) path parameters or performing subsequent path association. To quantify the uncertainty of the estimated positions, we develop a split conformal prediction (SCP) based calibration method that constructs angle-range predicted regions with finite-sample simultaneous coverage guarantees. Numerical results show that the proposed framework effectively controls the risk of source underestimation, while providing improved positioning accuracy with tighter predicted regions than benchmarks given the same target coverage levels.

title: Smart Model Routing for Order-of-Magnitude LLM Cost Reduction
comment: 35 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) deliver the strongest response quality but carry per-token prices often more than an order of magnitude above those of smaller, task-adequate models. Smart model routing addresses this mismatch by assigning each query to the cheapest model expected to answer it adequately, rather than sending every request to the most capable, most expensive endpoint. This paper develops a formal cost-quality optimization framework for routing -- including a derived optimal threshold-policy structure, a calibration-versus-discrimination distinction, a cascade breakeven condition, and a sensitivity analysis over price ratio and traffic skew -- situates that framework against the principal routing architectures and the signals used to estimate query difficulty, and works through a numerical example showing how a calibrated router can reduce blended inference cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to an always-frontier deployment under specific, stated pricing and traffic assumptions, reporting both the gross reduction from routing policy alone and the net figure with the router's own overhead priced in. We situate this figure against the range reported by published routing systems (roughly 2x to frontier-level accuracy at one-fifth the cost), and close with the practical risks -- under- and over-routing, aggregate quality constraints masking segment-level harm, calibration without discrimination, calibration drift, prompt injection into routing signals, and operational failures such as tier outages and multi-provider price variation -- that determine whether the savings materialize in production. The analysis is primarily analytical, complemented by a GSM8K evaluation of the cascade framework (Section 5), validated (Section 5.2); extending the evaluation across tasks and model families is future work.

title: Starscream: Reimagining LLM Sharding on AMD Instinct GPUs with GPU Partitioning
summary: As GPU accelerators grow larger to meet rising compute demands, they exhibit increasingly pronounced non-uniform memory access (NUMA) characteristics that challenge existing LLM frameworks. Chiplet-based architectures provide a practical path to larger GPUs while mitigating manufacturing yield constraints. Modern GPUs such as AMD Instinct MI300X employs such a multi-die design, and further offer GPU partitioning capabilities, partitioning a single physical GPU into multiple logical devices with NUMA-aware memory domains, promising faster kernel launches, and reduced memory access latencies with improved locality. However, current parallelization strategies, designed for homogeneous GPU topologies, when applied under partitioning, extend its unidimensional sharding causing significant performance degradation. Three bottlenecks emerge: (1) memory redundancy; (2) arithmetic intensity collapse; (3) communication overhead from flat collectives. We present Starscream, a rethinking of LLM sharding for the chiplet era. Rather than stretching inter-GPU sharding thinner, Starscream adds intra-GPU sharding along an orthogonal dimension, grounded in three foundational principles: kernel shape preservation, memory redundancy elimination, and communication overhead minimization. These principles form the basis for extending any sharding strategy into the partitioning regime. We demonstrate their effectiveness using tensor parallelism as a case study. On AMD MI300X and MI355X, exploiting partitioning capabilities yields up to 4x speedup for attention and 1.43x for fused GEMMs compared to chiplet-oblivious baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of chiplet-aware designs. Starscream's principles generalize across sharding strategies and future architectures.

title: DexRemo: A Force-Sensing Hand Platform and Task Suite for Contact-Rich Removal Manipulation
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Robotics (T-RO), 2026. Project website: this https URL
summary: Many manipulation tasks require separating adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained targets. We study this setting as removal manipulation, where progress depends on evolving contact states that are only partially observable from vision and kinematics. We introduce DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario real-robot task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. To make multi-finger force observations easier to fuse, we express fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame, giving force components consistent geometric meaning across fingers and time. Using an Action Chunking Transformer backbone, policies fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force observations to predict closed-loop action chunks from demonstrations. Evaluation uses six core benchmark tasks for controlled fingertip-input and force-frame ablations, plus three extension scenarios for additional held-out coverage. Across these evaluations, the learned policies achieve consistent removal performance, and ablations show that wrist-frame forces, especially with fingertip pose, improve stability and generalization over local-frame force inputs and no-force baselines. Project website: this https URL

title: REWEAVE: Online Learning for Workload-Adaptive HNSW Indexes
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Full version with appendix
summary: Vector databases rely on Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) indexes for similarity search, but a graph built from data alone can be poorly matched to a skewed or changing query workload. We present REWEAVE (Reward-Guided Rewiring of Vector Graphs), an online index-maintenance method that learns edge utility from query feedback and periodically rewires the bottom layer within the original per-node degree cap. The method supports sparse exact-neighbor feedback combined with self-labels, and standard HNSW serving without learning overhead once adaptation is disabled. Under explicit assumptions we prove value-estimation and graph-stabilization guarantees. Under stationary skew, REWEAVE improves held-out recall by up to 23.3 percentage points over HNSW. In comparisons with query-aware baselines on up to 100M vectors, it achieves up to 3.3x NGFix's query throughput at recall@100 of 0.80. On Amazon-ESCI with query drift, it increases stream recall@100 from 0.745 to 0.979 with 34% fewer search distance computations than frozen HNSW. These results illustrate the potential to improve retrieval quality and reduce search effort within an existing graph-degree budget, while incurring additional work during adaptation.

title: Gradient-Aware AI Agents for Autonomous Turbulence Model Discovery via Differentiable CFD
summary: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.

title: CupOFMoCA: Coupled Objective-Guided Discrete Flows for Molecular Conjugate Assembly
comment: Published at NeurIPS 2026. (Proceedings of the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, Sydney, Australia)
summary: Molecular conjugates, including PROTACs and peptide-drug conjugates (PDCs), derive their function from the joint behavior of multiple coupled components, yet most generative approaches design these components independently and combine them only after generation. Such staged pipelines ignore cross-component dependencies and often produce conjugates that are chemically invalid, fall outside empirical conjugate distributions, or lose function upon assembly. In this work, we introduce Coupled Objective-Guided Discrete Flows for Molecular Conjugate Assembly (CupOFMoCA), a discrete generative method that enforces cross-component chemical constraints during conjugate generation. CupOFMoCA restricts guided updates to chemically feasible conjugate states and reweights local transitions using molecular design objectives. Across three PDC systems, coupled generation achieved 100% conjugation validity among valid peptides and increased valid yield over matched post-hoc filtering, with comparable predicted binding scores across the full valid sets. In three-seed evaluations of three PROTAC systems, CupOFMoCA achieved the highest assembly validity on two systems and generated more assembly-valid molecules per second than the evaluated baselines. We further evaluated the generated PROTACs with post-hoc DegradeMaster scoring and explicit-solvent molecular dynamics, supporting their predicted activity and conformational properties. Together, these results establish CupOFMoCA as an efficient generator of molecular conjugates, supporting therapeutic development via coordinated control of assembly and molecular properties.

title: Calibrated Early Termination with Bounded Optimality Gaps for Constrained Vector Search
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Code available at this https URL
summary: Vector search over learned embeddings is the retrieval layer of recommendation and retrieval-augmented generation, and many applications cap how many answer items one category may contribute. Graph indexes answer a query by best-first traversal, and where it stops determines its cost and whether its answer is exact. We study early termination for such constrained $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) queries, with plain $k$-NN as a special case, and seek the cheapest stopping rule whose answer is exact with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$. Learned early-termination methods instead target average recall, which does not guarantee exact answers. Multiple testing can calibrate any parameterized stopping rule to our target, but it cannot tell how much a better rule with the same risk and observations would save. Answering this needs a lower bound on the optimum of a rule family too large to enumerate, valid for the query population. Our key idea is to declare the observations a rule may use and to consider every rule monotone in them. Risk-constrained stopping then becomes a linear program over an order polytope, whose Lagrangian minimizers form a nested chain of staircase rules computed exactly by dynamic programming. Fixed-sequence binomial tests along this chain calibrate our rule, CaST, whose failure probability is at most $\varepsilon$ with confidence $1-\delta$. Lagrangian weak duality bounds the optimum of the declared class from below at all risk levels at once, without a union bound over the rules. On two datasets of one million items each, CaST replayed on logged searches costs at most 1.132 times the class optimum for risk levels from 0.03 to 0.10, at 95% joint confidence per setting. Larger savings thus need a rule outside the class. At a common risk target on held-out queries, CaST is faster than every other calibrated rule we time, which take 4.8% to 45.5% more mean time.

title: Generative AI models for exploring diffusion dynamics from multi-frame particle tracking
summary: Particle-based volumetric flow measurement techniques have proven their efficacy in quantitatively assessing the dynamic characteristics of unsteady flows within the realm of fluid mechanics. Despite recent advances in multi-frame particle tracking, an open challenge in this area is maintaining trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences, where inter-frame displacements are large. In this work, we develop DiffTR-Flow3D, a diffusion-based model that estimates flow motion from spatiotemporal three-dimensional particle recordings via a stochastic diffusion process. DiffTR-Flow3D conditions the diffusion process with both global and local particle dynamics and enhances flow estimation by leveraging historical particle trajectories. Extensive experiments, including numerical simulations and real-world measurements, demonstrate that DiffTR-Flow3D achieves state-of-the-art displacement estimation accuracy compared with learning-based flow estimators, and, when integrated into particle tracking pipelines, substantially improves their long-term tracking performance, while exhibiting robustness and generalization across diverse flow patterns. This work is expected to provide fluid researchers with an effective tool for the consistent and precise analysis of particle trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences with large inter-frame displacements.

title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
comment: 24 pages, 10 tables, 6 figures
summary: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level this http URL::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables
summary: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.

title: HybridCT: ML Accelerated Tomography for Climate Relevant 3D Cloud Observations
summary: Low-level clouds are one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate predictions, partly because we lack detailed three-dimensional (3D) measurements of their internal structure. Here, we present HybridCT, a cloud tomographic reconstruction scheme accelerated by machine learning (ML) that recovers 3D cloud extinction directly from passive multi-angle observations. An ML emulator maps radiances from multiple viewing angles to cloud optical thickness (COT), producing path-integrated projections, and a Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) explicitly inverts these projections to retrieve 3D extinction. Training observations are generated from synthetic 3D cloud fields using radiative transfer simulations for nine viewing angles between $\pm$70$^{\circ}$. HybridCT reconstructs extinction with RMSE 13.3 km$^{-1}$ in 3.5 s, compared to 22.7 km$^{-1}$ in approx. 30 min for the state-of-the-art physics-based tomography framework AT3D, a speedup exceeding 500$\times$. HybridCT thus provides a scalable route toward large-scale observations of 3D cloud structure relevant to radiative-budget interpretation and evaluation of high-resolution cloud simulations.

title: BlinkMimic: Training a Humanoid Motion Tracker in Minutes on a Single GPU
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Whole-body motion tracking lets a humanoid robot follow reference motions, but training a tracking policy for a library of motions has usually taken hours of GPU time. SuperMimic showed that the policy can instead be trained by backpropagating through a world model learned from parallel simulation, and InstantTrack added Muon updates, a residual policy around the reference and an averaged deployed policy. We build on both and present BlinkMimic, a recipe that makes this training faster. On a simulated Unitree G1, BlinkMimic trains one policy for all 40 LAFAN1 clips in 3.4 minutes on a single RTX 4090, measured until three consecutive checkpoints reach a normalized return of at least 0.82 with no failed clip (mean of three seeds). We split training time into the cost of an iteration, the iterations needed to fit the motions, and the iterations needed to remove the last failures, and assign each component, inherited or new, to one of these terms. The new components are a step size that decreases once training has progressed, resets directed by failures of the deployed policy under deployment conditions, and GPU graph capture of the whole iteration. A leave-one-out ablation with three seeds per component shows which term each component affects, and further measurements of the gradient, the update rule and the failure cases explain these effects. Code and per-seed results are available at this https URL.

title: TAPES: Terminal Adjoint-Propagated Error Scheduling for Financial Diffusion Samplers
comment: 9 pages. Accepted at the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF 2026)
summary: Financial diffusion samplers are often reused with a small number of function evaluations (NFE) inside scenario and risk pipelines, where numerical time-grid error can distort terminal quantities such as covariances, tails, and drawdown proxies. We study offline grid construction for a frozen probability-flow ODE: the score network, conditioning, Euler solver, report normalization, and deployment NFE remain fixed. TAPES (Terminal Adjoint-Propagated Error Scheduling) estimates signed local defects by Richardson comparisons, transports them through the remaining discrete flow and a terminal-report adjoint, and optimizes the squared norm of their sum before a capped direct refinement. We show that this transported signed sum is the first-order terminal-report error and quantify, under an aligned-defect model, the inefficiency of diagonal criteria. Across six budgets on a regime-switching simulation and chronologically held-out Mag7 contexts, TAPES gives the lowest design- and audit-report errors in all 24 dataset--budget--report rows within the reported five-pipeline panel. Cross-budget mean relative audit-error reductions are about 10--11% on Regime-SV and about 1% on Mag7, with Bonferroni intervals excluding zero; all displayed winners persist under a doubled-resolution reference, and a small Regime-SV Heun probe preserves the TAPES-first audit ordering. TAPES changes only the offline schedule and retains the prescribed deployment NFE; claims concern numerical fidelity to frozen generators.

title: Similarity-Guided Optimization Strategies for Approximate Network Symmetry Detection
comment: 90 pages, 15 figures and 2 tables in the main text; supplementary material with 64 figures and 7 tables included
summary: Symmetry in complex networks is a structural property with broad implications for network function, dynamics, and robustness. While classical approaches rely on exact automorphisms and thus remain highly sensitive to small perturbations, recent work of Liu has introduced approximate formulations that relax the strict invariance condition and recast symmetry detection as an optimization problem over permutations. We investigate how node-level similarity information can be used to bias the search toward structurally plausible vertex correspondences, with network centralities serving as one interpretable instance. Building on this perspective, we adapt simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, tabu search, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution and the quadratic symmetry approximator to this problem, add similarity guidance to each, and introduce Bilinear Approximate Symmetry Inference (BASIN), which learns a soft assignment matrix via bilinear embeddings. Using a unified evaluation pipeline, we compare their guided and unguided variants, BASIN and a random baseline on four synthetic graph families, structural brain connectomes, and three empirical networks with known automorphism groups. Node-similarity guidance is decisive where a planted orbit exists that the unguided search misses, and algorithm-dependent elsewhere, on synthetic and empirical networks alike.
